# Logger

> Structured logging for TelamonJS — one ILogger interface for browser, server and workers, with child loggers, timers, audit and perf extensions

Source: apps/docs/content/docs/packages/logger.mdx

`@telamonjs/logger` (current version: <PkgVersion pkg='logger' />) is
the shared logging system of the TelamonJS ecosystem — one `ILogger` interface for
Node.js, browser and SSR, with structured context, correlation IDs, performance
timers and audit trails. It is also the logger injected into
[`@telamonjs/queue`](/docs/queue/logging).

```bash
pnpm add @telamonjs/logger
```

## Quick start

```typescript
import { logger } from '@telamonjs/logger'

// Standard levels (RFC 5424)
logger.debug('Debugging info', { component: 'UserService' })
logger.info('User logged in', { userId: '123' })
logger.warn('API rate limit approaching', { remaining: 10 })
logger.error('Payment failed', { orderId: '456', error: err.message })
logger.fatal('Database connection lost')

// TelamonJS extensions
logger.success('User created successfully', { userId: '789' })
logger.perf('Query executed', 1234, { query: 'SELECT * FROM users' })
```

The default `logger` instance is a `ConsoleLogger` whose level is auto-detected
from `LOG_LEVEL`/`NODE_ENV`.

## ILogger interface

Every adapter implements the same contract:

```typescript
interface ILogger {
  // Standard levels
  debug(message: string, context?: LogContext): void
  info(message: string, context?: LogContext): void
  warn(message: string, context?: LogContext): void
  error(message: string, context?: LogContext): void
  fatal(message: string, context?: LogContext): void

  // TelamonJS extensions
  success(message: string, context?: LogContext): void
  audit(action: AuditAction, context?: AuditContext): void
  perf(label: string, durationMs: number, context?: LogContext): void

  // Context management
  child(context: LogContext): ILogger
  withRequestId(requestId: string): ILogger
  withUser(user: { id: string; email?: string; role?: string }): ILogger

  // Timers
  startTimer(label?: string): LogTimer

  // Configuration
  setLevel(level: LogLevel): void
  getLevel(): LogLevel
  isLevelEnabled(level: LogLevel): boolean
}
```

Levels: `FATAL(0)` → `ERROR(1)` → `WARN(2)` → `INFO(3)` → `DEBUG(4)` → `TRACE(5)`.
`LOG_LEVEL` env var overrides; otherwise `NODE_ENV` picks a sensible default
(development → DEBUG, production → INFO, test → ERROR).

## Factories

Environment-specific factory functions:

```typescript
import {
  createLogger,
  createServerLogger,
  createBrowserLogger,
  createWorkerLogger,
  createTestLogger,
} from '@telamonjs/logger'

// Level from LOG_LEVEL / NODE_ENV unless you pass one
const logger = createLogger({
  level: LogLevel.INFO,
  context: { service: 'my-app' },
})

createServerLogger() // Server Components, API routes: JSON lines
createBrowserLogger() // colorized console output
createWorkerLogger({ context: { jobId, jobName } }) // background jobs: no ANSI colors
createTestLogger() // silent no-op for tests
```

The factories are configured through `LoggerConfig`: `level`, `enabled`, `context`, `format`,
`colorize`, `showTimestamps`, `showLevel`, `showContext`. `enabled: false` returns a
`NoOpLogger`; otherwise `format` picks the output:

| `format`             | Logger          | Output                                                    |
| -------------------- | --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `'simple'` (default) | `ConsoleLogger` | human-readable text                                       |
| `'json'`             | `ConsoleLogger` | one JSON object per line, for log aggregators             |
| `'pretty'`           | `PrettyLogger`  | icons and colors for CLIs                                 |

`createServerLogger()` defaults to `'json'`; pass `format: 'simple'` for text. A JSON line holds
`timestamp` (ISO 8601), `level` (lowercase), `message` and, when there is any, `context`:

```json
{"timestamp":"2026-01-01T12:00:00.000Z","level":"info","message":"User created","context":{"userId":"123"}}
```

Error and fatal lines go to `console.error`, warnings to `console.warn`, the rest to `console.log`.

## Adapters

| Adapter         | Use case                                              | Extras                                       |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `ConsoleLogger` | Development and browser                               | colorize, timestamps, context display        |
| `PrettyLogger`  | CLIs                                                  | `banner()`, `step()`, `newLine()`            |
| `BrowserLogger` | Client components                                     | `transport`, `flush()`, `getBuffer()`, `clearBuffer()` |
| `NoOpLogger`    | Tests, benchmarks                                     | silent                                       |

<Callout type='info' title='One entry point, console output'>
  Everything is exported from one browser-safe entry point, `@telamonjs/logger`. The adapters
  write to the console; the only transport is the opt-in browser one below. To send logs to an
  aggregator or an error tracker, implement `ILogger` (or extend `BaseLogger`) in your app — see
  [Custom sinks](/docs/queue/logging#custom-sinks-sentry-datadog-).
</Callout>

### Shipping browser logs to your backend

`createBrowserLogger({ transport })` returns a `BrowserLogger` that still writes to the console
and also ships entries in batches:

```typescript
'use client'
import { createBrowserLogger, LogLevel } from '@telamonjs/logger'

export const logger = createBrowserLogger({
  transport: {
    endpoint: '/api/logs', // POST { logs: BrowserLogEntry[] } as JSON
    level: LogLevel.WARN, // default: WARN, ERROR and FATAL
  },
})
```

| Option            | Default         | Meaning                                                                 |
| ----------------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `endpoint`        | —               | URL that receives the batches (same-origin is simplest)                 |
| `send`            | —               | Your own function per batch, instead of `fetch`/`sendBeacon`            |
| `level`           | `LogLevel.WARN` | Least severe level shipped; the console still follows the logger level |
| `batchSize`       | `20`            | Ship as soon as this many entries are queued                            |
| `flushIntervalMs` | `5000`          | Ship what is queued on this interval                                    |
| `includePii`      | `false`         | Keep context keys that usually hold personal data                       |

Each `BrowserLogEntry` holds `level`, `levelName`, `message`, `timestamp` (ISO 8601) and
`context`. By default, context keys that usually hold personal data (`userEmail`, `ip`,
`userAgent`, tokens, passwords, cookies, phone, CPF…) are dropped at any depth; messages are sent
as written, so keep personal data out of them. When the tab is hidden or closed, the queue goes
out through `navigator.sendBeacon`. Failed deliveries are dropped, never retried or thrown. Child
loggers share the parent's queue. On the server (no `window`) the transport is inactive.

## Context management

```typescript
// Child logger — context merged into every log
const userLogger = logger.child({ userId: user.id, email: user.email })
userLogger.info('Profile updated')

// Request correlation
const requestLogger = logger.withRequestId(req.headers['x-request-id'])
requestLogger.info('Request started')
requestLogger.info('Request completed') // same requestId — traceable

// Performance timers
const timer = logger.startTimer('Database query')
const users = await prisma.user.findMany()
timer.done('Users fetched') // "Users fetched (1234ms)"
```

### Audit trails

```typescript
logger.audit('user.created', {
  userId: newUser.id,
  resource: 'user',
  resourceId: newUser.id,
  changes: { email: { before: null, after: newUser.email } },
  compliance: ['GDPR', 'LGPD'],
})
```

Audit entries are compliance records: `audit()` ignores the level filter and writes even under
`level: 'warn'` or `'error'`, at INFO severity. Only a disabled logger (`enabled: false`,
`createTestLogger()`) drops them.

## Best practices

```typescript
// ✅ Structured context, not string concatenation
logger.info('User logged in', { userId: user.id })

// ✅ Scoped child loggers per request/job
const requestLogger = logger.withRequestId(requestId)

// ✅ The error level for errors, not info
logger.error('Payment failed', { error: err.message })

// ❌ Never log sensitive data — the logger does not redact anything
logger.info('User password', { password: user.password })
```

## Related

- [Queue logging](/docs/queue/logging) — injecting an `ILogger` into the queue system

---

# Queue

> Production-ready background job system for TelamonJS — BullMQ, Redis, type-safe jobs, scheduling, DLQ and monitoring

Source: apps/docs/content/docs/queue/index.mdx

`@telamonjs/queue` (current version: <PkgVersion pkg='queue' />) is the
background job system of the TelamonJS ecosystem, built on **BullMQ** with a **Redis**
backend.

## Features

- **Type-safe jobs** — `Job<TData, TResult>` generics, compile-time safety
- **Job flows (DAGs)** — complex job dependencies via `FlowProducer`
- **Scheduling** — cron patterns, human-readable helpers, timezone support
- **Retry strategies** — exponential, fixed and custom backoff
- **Priorities** — semantic `JobPriority` enum (CRITICAL → DEFERRED)
- **Dead Letter Queue** — permanently failed jobs preserved for inspection and retry
- **Bulk operations** — `addBulk`, `retryBulk`, `removeBulk`, drain, clean
- **Monitoring** — Bull Board dashboard, Prometheus metrics, health endpoints
- **Structured logging** — injectable `ILogger` from `@telamonjs/logger`
- **Graceful shutdown** — `drainAll()` lets active jobs finish, `close()` closes
  workers, then queues; all state in Redis, so worker processes scale horizontally

## Quick Start

<Steps>
<Step>

### Install

```bash
pnpm add @telamonjs/queue
```

Requires Node.js 22.12+ and Redis 6+ (`docker run -d -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine`).

Every dependency comes with the package; what loads depends on the import. The
root entry is the core (BullMQ, ioredis, the job engine), with no Express or
Bull Board. `@telamonjs/queue/dashboard` loads Express and the Bull Board UI;
`@telamonjs/queue/metrics` holds the Prometheus collectors.

</Step>
<Step>

### Define a job

```typescript title="jobs/send-email.ts"
import { Job } from '@telamonjs/queue'

interface EmailData {
  to: string
  subject: string
  body: string
}

export class SendEmailJob extends Job<EmailData, void> {
  name = 'send-email' as const

  options = {
    attempts: 3,
    backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000 },
    timeout: 30000,
  }

  async process(data: EmailData): Promise<void> {
    await sendEmail(data)
  }

  async onFailed(error: Error): Promise<void> {
    // cleanup / alerting
  }
}
```

Jobs can also declare a `schedule` (cron) and a `validate()` hook — see
[Scheduling](/docs/queue/scheduling) and [Validation](/docs/queue/validation).

</Step>
<Step>

### Set up the QueueManager

```typescript title="queue.ts"
import { QueueManager } from '@telamonjs/queue'
import { createLogger } from '@telamonjs/logger'
import { SendEmailJob } from './jobs/send-email'

const queueManager = new QueueManager({
  redis: {
    host: process.env.REDIS_HOST || 'localhost',
    port: parseInt(process.env.REDIS_PORT || '6379'),
  },
  prefix: 'myapp',
  logger: createLogger({ context: { service: 'myapp-queue' } }),
})

queueManager.register(SendEmailJob)

await queueManager.createWorkers({ concurrency: 5 })
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Add jobs

```typescript
// Single job
await queueManager.add(SendEmailJob, {
  to: 'user@example.com',
  subject: 'Welcome!',
  body: 'Welcome to our platform',
})

// With options
await queueManager.add(SendEmailJob, data, {
  priority: 1, // see JobPriority
  delay: 5000,
})

// Bulk (one Redis round-trip)
await queueManager.addBulk(SendEmailJob, [
  { data: { to: 'user1@example.com', subject: 'News', body: '...' } },
  { data: { to: 'user2@example.com', subject: 'News', body: '...' } },
])
```

</Step>
</Steps>

## Architecture

The `QueueManager` orchestrates the whole system: it holds the **job registry**,
creates one **queue** and one **worker** per registered job, and manages lifecycle
(pause/resume/close). All state lives in Redis, so multiple worker instances scale
horizontally.

| Component            | Role                                                                     |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Job`                | Abstract base class for type-safe job definitions                        |
| `QueueManager`       | Main orchestrator: registry, queues, workers, stats, shutdown            |
| `Queue`              | Typed wrapper over a BullMQ queue; `getRawQueue()` is the escape hatch   |
| `Worker`             | Runs a job's hooks and `process()` for each picked-up job                |
| `DeadLetterQueue`    | Storage for permanently failed jobs                                      |
| `FlowProducer`       | Job dependency graphs (DAGs)                                             |
| `QueueRegistry`      | BullMQ queues over **one** shared Redis connection, for code outside a `QueueManager` (API routes, a scheduler process) |
| `JobConfigStore` (`/job-config`) | Per-job config in Redis (enabled, cron, priority, concurrency, timeout) plus a change history |
| `SchedulerReconciler` (`/scheduler`) | Keeps BullMQ job schedulers in sync with the `JobConfigStore` |

### Data flow

**Adding a job.** `queueManager.add(JobClass, data, options)`:

1. instantiates the class to read its `name`, and throws `JobNotFoundError` if it
   was never registered;
2. merges the options, most specific last: the manager's `defaultJobOptions`, then
   the class's `options`, then the call-site `options`;
3. validates the merged options (`InvalidJobOptionsError`);
4. hands the job to BullMQ, which stores it in Redis under the manager's `prefix`.

**Processing a job.** A worker picks the job up (BullMQ moves it atomically from
*waiting* to *active*) and runs, in order: `validate(data)`, `transform(data)`,
`onActive(data)`, `process(data)` and `onCompleted(result)`. Every step except
`process()` is optional.

```text
added ──▶ waiting ──▶ active ──▶ completed   onCompleted · kept: newest 100 (removeOnComplete)
             ▲          │
             │          ├──▶ failed attempt  onFailed · retried while attempts remain
             └──────────┘
                        ├──▶ failed          last attempt · kept: newest 500 (removeOnFail) · copied to the DLQ
                        └──▶ stalled         worker died mid-job · onStalled · BullMQ re-queues it
```

**Concurrency.** `createWorkers({ concurrency: 5 })` lets each worker run 5 jobs of
its queue at once on the Node.js event loop; `concurrencyPerQueue` overrides the
value per job name. Capacity adds up across processes: three worker processes with
`concurrency: 5` run up to 15 jobs of that queue in parallel.

**Timeout.** An attempt that runs past its `timeout` fails with `JobTimeoutError`
and frees its concurrency slot; the normal retry and DLQ path then applies. The
deadline covers `validate`, `transform`, `onActive` and `process`. The value comes
from the job's `JobConfigStore` config (via `createWorkersFromConfig`, or
`timeoutPerQueue` on `createWorkers`), else the `timeout` the job was enqueued
with, else the class's `options.timeout`. `process(data, ctx)` receives
`ctx.signal`, which aborts at the deadline.

<Callout type='warn' title='A timeout does not stop a handler that ignores ctx.signal'>
  JavaScript cannot kill a running `process()`. After the timeout, a handler that
  ignores `ctx.signal` keeps running in the background while the retry starts, so
  the same job can run twice at once, above the worker's concurrency. A handler
  with side effects (charges, emails, writes) must stop when `ctx.signal` aborts
  (pass it to `fetch` and other I/O, check `signal.aborted` between steps) or be
  safe to run twice.
</Callout>

### Design decisions

- **BullMQ on Redis.** BullMQ provides atomic job state, priorities, delays, rate
  limiting, repeatable jobs and the Bull Board UI; Redis is fast, well understood
  operationally, and shared by every process. The cost is one more service to run.
- **Jobs are classes.** The generics on `Job<TData, TResult>` carry the payload type
  from the class to `add()`, so a wrong payload is a compile error. A job is plain
  code: instantiate it and call `process()` to test it. Defaults live on the base
  class: 3 attempts, exponential backoff from 1 second, keep the newest 100
  completed and 500 failed jobs.
- **A typed wrapper with an escape hatch.** `Queue` hides BullMQ's type machinery
  behind a small API and casts at that boundary. Anything it does not wrap
  (repeatables, Bull Board adapters) goes through `getRawQueue()`.
- **Producers and workers are separate.** Every process registers the same jobs;
  only the worker processes call `createWorkers()`. Web servers and workers then
  scale, deploy and fail independently.

  ```typescript
  // shared: queue.ts
  export const queueManager = new QueueManager({ redis, prefix: 'myapp' })
  queueManager.register(SendEmailJob)
  queueManager.register(GenerateReportJob)

  // web process: only enqueues
  await queueManager.add(SendEmailJob, { to, subject, body })

  // worker process: also processes
  await queueManager.createWorkers({ concurrency: 5 })
  process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
    await queueManager.close() // closes workers, then queues
    process.exit(0)
  })
  ```

- **Fail, retry, keep the evidence.** A failing job is retried with backoff rather
  than left hanging. After the last attempt it stays inspectable: in the failed set
  (Bull Board, retry from the dashboard) and in the
  [Dead Letter Queue](/docs/queue/dead-letter-queue). See
  [Error Handling](/docs/queue/error-handling#failures-inside-a-job).
- **Three monitoring layers.** Bull Board for people (inspect and retry one job),
  Prometheus for alerts (failure rate, backlog, latency), health endpoints for the
  orchestrator (restart or stop routing to an unhealthy worker).
- **Runtime config in Redis, not in code.** Enabling a job or changing its cron is
  an edit in the [Jobs Dashboard](/docs/queue/dashboard), stored in the
  `JobConfigStore` and applied by the `SchedulerReconciler`, with no redeploy. See
  [Scheduling](/docs/queue/scheduling).
- **One Redis connection for the scheduler.** `QueueRegistry` reuses its queues over
  a single connection, so a reconcile loop or an API route never opens a connection
  per tick or per request.

### Job flows (DAGs)

```typescript
import { FlowProducer } from '@telamonjs/queue'

const flow = new FlowProducer({ queueManager })

const node = await flow.add({
  name: 'import-flow',
  job: 'generate-report', // the parent runs last; jobs by registered name
  data: { importId },
  children: [
    { job: 'import-rows', data: { importId } },
    { job: 'sync-search-index', data: { importId } },
  ],
})
```

BullMQ runs a flow from the leaves up: the children run (in parallel) and the
parent waits in *waiting-children* until all of them complete.

`add()` returns the created tree (BullMQ `JobNode`): `node.job.id` is the root job's
id, so `await flow.getFlow(node.job.id!, node.job.queueName)` reads the flow back
with each job's current state. Every node gets the same options as
`queueManager.add()` would give it: the manager's `defaultJobOptions`, then the job
class's `options`, then the node's own `options`.

### QueueManager API at a glance

```typescript
queueManager.register(SendEmailJob) // one call per job class

await queueManager.add(SendEmailJob, data, options)
await queueManager.addBulk(SendEmailJob, [...])

await queueManager.createWorkers({ concurrency: 5 })

const stats = await queueManager.getStats()
// { 'send-email': { waiting: 10, active: 5, completed: 100, ... } }

await queueManager.pauseAll()
await queueManager.resumeAll()
await queueManager.close()
```

- **Jobs Dashboard** — React dashboard from `@telamonjs/ui/queue` and the
  embeddable Bull Board server from `@telamonjs/queue/dashboard`. See
  [Dashboard](/docs/queue/dashboard).
- **Prometheus metrics** — `QueueMetrics` / `OptimizedQueueMetrics` from
  `@telamonjs/queue/metrics`. See [Metrics](/docs/queue/metrics).
- **Health checks** — `/live`, `/ready` and `/health` endpoints for Kubernetes
  liveness/readiness probes.

## Recipes

### Email with validation and alerting

```typescript
import { z } from 'zod'
import { Job } from '@telamonjs/queue'

const EmailSchema = z.object({
  to: z.string().email(),
  subject: z.string().min(1),
  body: z.string(),
})
type EmailData = z.infer<typeof EmailSchema>

export class SendEmailJob extends Job<EmailData, void> {
  name = 'send-email' as const

  options = {
    attempts: 3,
    backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 2000 }, // 2s, 4s, 8s
    removeOnComplete: 100,
  }

  async validate(data: unknown): Promise<void> {
    EmailSchema.parse(data)
  }

  async process(data: EmailData): Promise<void> {
    await mailer.send(data)
  }

  async onFailed(error: Error): Promise<void> {
    await alerts.notify(`send-email attempt failed: ${error.message}`)
  }
}
```

### Long report, then notify

Give slow jobs an explicit `timeout` and fewer attempts, and enqueue the follow-up
job when they finish:

```typescript
import { Job } from '@telamonjs/queue'
import { queueManager } from './queue'

interface ReportData {
  userEmail: string
  type: 'sales' | 'inventory'
  from: string
  to: string
}

interface ReportResult {
  fileUrl: string
  userEmail: string
}

export class GenerateReportJob extends Job<ReportData, ReportResult> {
  name = 'generate-report' as const

  options = {
    attempts: 2,
    timeout: 5 * 60 * 1000, // 5 minutes
    removeOnComplete: 50,
  }

  async process(data: ReportData): Promise<ReportResult> {
    const rows = await reports.fetch(data.type, data.from, data.to)
    const fileUrl = await storage.upload(await renderPdf(rows))
    return { fileUrl, userEmail: data.userEmail }
  }

  async onCompleted(result: ReportResult): Promise<void> {
    await queueManager.add(SendEmailJob, {
      to: result.userEmail,
      subject: 'Your report is ready',
      body: `Download: ${result.fileUrl}`,
    })
  }
}
```

`onCompleted` receives only the result, so return whatever the follow-up needs.

### Import that must not run twice

An import that writes rows is not safe to retry from the start. Run it once, record
per-row failures in the result, and report them instead of throwing:

```typescript
import { Job } from '@telamonjs/queue'

interface ImportResult {
  total: number
  imported: number
  errors: Array<{ row: number; error: string }>
}

export class ImportCsvJob extends Job<{ fileUrl: string }, ImportResult> {
  name = 'import-csv' as const

  options = {
    attempts: 1, // never retry an import
    timeout: 30 * 60 * 1000,
  }

  async process({ fileUrl }: { fileUrl: string }): Promise<ImportResult> {
    const rows = await parseCsv(fileUrl)
    const result: ImportResult = { total: rows.length, imported: 0, errors: [] }

    for (const [index, row] of rows.entries()) {
      try {
        await importRow(row)
        result.imported++
      } catch (error) {
        result.errors.push({ row: index + 1, error: String(error) })
      }
    }
    return result
  }
}
```

### Nightly cleanup

A recurring job declares its cron in `configDefaults` and is scheduled by the
`SchedulerReconciler` — see [Scheduling](/docs/queue/scheduling):

```typescript
import { Job } from '@telamonjs/queue'

export class CleanupTempFilesJob extends Job<void, number> {
  name = 'cleanup-temp-files' as const
  configDefaults = { cronPattern: '0 2 * * *', enabled: true } // every day at 02:00

  async process(): Promise<number> {
    return files.deleteTemporaryOlderThan(30) // days; returns the count
  }
}
```

## Testing

### Unit tests: call the job directly

A job is a class, so most tests need no Redis: instantiate it and call `validate()`
and `process()` with the collaborators mocked.

```typescript title="jobs/send-email.test.ts"
import { describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest'
import { SendEmailJob } from './send-email'
import { mailer } from '../lib/mailer'

vi.mock('../lib/mailer', () => ({ mailer: { send: vi.fn() } }))

describe('SendEmailJob', () => {
  it('rejects invalid data', async () => {
    await expect(
      new SendEmailJob().validate({ to: 'not-an-email', subject: '', body: '' })
    ).rejects.toThrow()
  })

  it('sends the email', async () => {
    const data = { to: 'user@example.com', subject: 'Hi', body: 'Hello' }
    await new SendEmailJob().process(data)
    expect(mailer.send).toHaveBeenCalledWith(data)
  })
})
```

Hooks are plain methods too: call `onFailed(new Error('boom'))` directly to test
the alerting. Calling `process()` never triggers the hooks; the worker does that.

### Integration tests: a real Redis

```typescript title="queue.integration.test.ts"
import { afterAll, beforeAll, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest'
import { QueueManager } from '@telamonjs/queue'
import { NoOpLogger } from '@telamonjs/logger'
import { SendEmailJob } from './jobs/send-email'

let queueManager: QueueManager

beforeAll(() => {
  queueManager = new QueueManager({
    redis: { host: 'localhost', port: 6379, db: 1 }, // a db the app does not use
    prefix: `test-${process.pid}`,
    logger: new NoOpLogger(),
    enableDLQ: false,
  })
  queueManager.register(SendEmailJob)
})

afterAll(() => queueManager.close())

it('processes an enqueued job', async () => {
  await queueManager.createWorkers({ concurrency: 1 })
  await queueManager.add(SendEmailJob, { to: 'user@example.com', subject: 'Hi', body: 'Hello' })

  await vi.waitFor(
    async () => {
      const stats = await queueManager.getStats()
      expect(stats['send-email']?.completed).toBe(1)
    },
    { timeout: 5000 }
  )
})
```

- **One registration per job per process.** The job registry is shared by every
  `QueueManager` in the process, so registering the same class twice throws
  `JobAlreadyRegisteredError`. Create the manager once per test file (Vitest
  isolates test files by default).
- **Isolate the keys.** A dedicated Redis `db` and a unique `prefix` keep test runs
  from seeing each other's jobs.
- **Poll, don't sleep.** Wait for the stats with `vi.waitFor` instead of a fixed
  `setTimeout`.

## Best Practices

- **Keep jobs idempotent** — jobs should be safe to retry
- **Validate input** — use the `validate()` hook with a Zod schema
- **Use bulk operations** for batches — one Redis round-trip instead of N
- **Clean old jobs** — set `removeOnComplete` / `removeOnFail` and run periodic cleans
- **Secure Redis and the dashboard** — password-protect both, never expose Redis publicly
- **Monitor queue sizes and the DLQ** — alert on backlog and failure growth

# Field Types

> All 36 field types registered in the telamonjs-ui field system

Source: apps/docs/content/docs/reference/field-types.mdx

Reference for all **36 field types** registered in the telamonjs-ui field system (list them with `getAvailableFieldTypes()`). Use these in `FormSection.fields[].type`.

<Callout type='error' title="'select' does NOT exist">
  There is no `'select'` field type. **Always use `'relationship'`** for
  dropdowns.
</Callout>

```typescript
// ❌ NEVER use 'select' (does not exist) — and there is no `options` prop either
{ name: 'category', type: 'select', options: [...] }

// ✅ ALWAYS use 'relationship'; options come from `loadField`
{
  name: 'category',
  label: 'Category',
  type: 'relationship',
  loadField: async () => [
    { value: 'a', label: 'Category A' },
    { value: 'b', label: 'Category B' },
  ],
}
```

`loadField` has the type `() => Promise<IOption[]> | ((search, id, dependsOn?) => Promise<IOption[]>)`:
return the options directly (`IOption` is `{ value: string | number; label }`), or return a
search function for server-side filtering of large lists. Pair it with `dependsOn` to reload
options when another field changes.

---

## Quick Reference

| Field Type | When to Use | Special Props |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `'text'` | Simple text | `placeholder` |
| `'email'` | Validated email | `placeholder` |
| `'password'` | Password | `placeholder` |
| `'textarea'` | Long text | `placeholder`, `rows` (default 4) |
| `'number'` | Integer | `placeholder` |
| `'float'` | Decimal number | `placeholder` |
| `'boolean'` | On/off switch | `default` |
| `'checkbox'` | Checkbox | `default` |
| `'date'` | Date | `minDate`, `maxDate` |
| `'datetime'` | Date + time | - |
| `'masked-datetime'` | Masked date/time | `mask` |
| **`'relationship'`** | **Dropdown / select** | `loadField`, `dependsOn` |
| `'multiselect'` | Multiple select | `loadField`, `dependsOn` |
| `'image'` | Image upload | `uploadFn`, `path` |
| `'file'` | File upload | `uploadFn`, `path`, `resolveUrl` |
| `'masked'` | Masked input (CPF, phone) | `mask`, `maskType` — see [Masks](#masks) |
| `'component'` | Custom component | `Component` |
| `'crud'` | Nested data 1:N | See [CRUD Field Pattern](/docs/patterns/crud-field) |
| `'hidden'` | Hidden field | - |

Every field also accepts `name`, `label`, `type`, `required`, `description`, `placeholder`,
`span`, `readOnly`, `default`, `editOnly` and `visibleWhen`.

### Additional Types (full registry)

| Field Type | Category | When to Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `'string'` | Text | Alias of `'text'` (same renderer) |
| `'currency'` | Number | Formatted monetary values |
| `'masked-date'` | Date/Time | Masked date (same renderer as `'date'`) |
| `'time'` | Date/Time | Time only (HH:mm) |
| `'daterange'` | Date/Time | Date interval (start/end) |
| `'month'` | Date/Time | Month picker (HTML5 `month` input) |
| `'week'` | Date/Time | Week picker (HTML5 `week` input) |
| `'fileupload'` | File | Upload with advanced UI (progress/drag-drop) |
| `'url'` | HTML5 | Validated URL (`url` input) |
| `'tel'` | HTML5 | Phone (`tel` input) |
| `'color'` | HTML5 | Color picker (`color` input) |
| `'range'` | HTML5 | Numeric slider (`range` input) |
| `'search'` | HTML5 | Search field (`search` input) |
| `'richtext'` | Advanced | Rich text editor (TipTap — lazy-loaded) |
| `'wizard'` | Advanced | Multi-step flow inside the form |
| `'svg'` | Special | SVG upload/preview |
| `'space'` | Special | Layout spacer (renders no input) |

---

## Masks

A `'masked'` field formats digits as they are typed. Give it a `maskType` preset, or your own
`mask` where each `_` is one digit:

| `maskType` | Mask |
| --- | --- |
| `'tel'` | `(__) ____-____`, switching to `(__) _____-____` at the 11th digit |
| `'cpf'` | `___.___.___-__` |
| `'cnpj'` | `__.___.___/____-__` (digits only) |
| `'cep'` | `_____-___` |

```typescript
{ name: 'document', label: 'CPF', type: 'masked', maskType: 'cpf' }
{ name: 'code', label: 'Code', type: 'masked', mask: '___-____' } // custom mask
```

A preset wins over `mask`; any other `maskType` value falls back to `mask`. The stored value is
the formatted text.

---

## Categories

| Category | Field Types |
| --- | --- |
| Text | `text`, `string`, `email`, `password`, `textarea`, `masked` |
| Number | `number`, `float`, `currency` |
| Boolean | `boolean`, `checkbox` |
| Date/Time | `date`, `datetime`, `masked-date`, `masked-datetime`, `time`, `daterange`, `month`, `week` |
| Select | `relationship`, `multiselect` |
| File | `image`, `file`, `fileupload` |
| HTML5 | `url`, `tel`, `color`, `range`, `search` |
| Advanced | `richtext`, `wizard` |
| Special | `component`, `crud`, `svg`, `space`, `hidden` |

---

## Field Width in BaseForm

BaseForm uses CSS Grid (not flexbox), so `className='w-full'` is ignored. Use `span` instead, matching the section `grid` value:

```typescript
// span must match the section grid value (default '2')
{ name: 'fullWidthField', type: 'relationship', span: '2' }
// For grid='3' sections, use span='3' for full width
```

# Decision Trees

> Which page, form, detail component, layout, chart or field type fits your case

Source: apps/docs/content/docs/reference.mdx

Short answers to "which one do I use?". Each tree ends at the page that documents
the choice.

## Create, edit and view

```
Where do create, edit and view happen?
│
├─ Default → dialogs on the list
│  └─ config.dialogs.create / edit / view, data from mutations.getForEdit / getForView
│
├─ The view has 6+ sections → dialogs.view.portal (section launcher in the dialog)
│
└─ The form or the view outgrows a dialog (very long form, own URL, sub-resources)
   └─ Standalone pages: CreatePage / EditPage, DetailLayout on an [id] page
```

See [Dialogs](/docs/patterns/dialogs), [Detail views](/docs/patterns/detail-page) and
[Standalone form pages](/docs/patterns/edit-page). `telamonjs lint` flags standalone
CRUD routes unless you opt out per file.

## Form component

```
Need a form?
│
├─ Create/edit of a CrudConfig module → nothing to pick: the dialogs render config.form
│
├─ A standalone page → CreatePage / EditPage (BaseFormPage for full control)
│
├─ A form inside your own layout
│  ├─ Creating → CreateForm
│  ├─ Editing  → EditForm (requires id + data)
│  └─ Neither  → Form
│
└─ A multi-step wizard, or form state read elsewhere on the page (live preview)
   ├─ Rendered from a Server Component page → ZustandFormServer
   └─ Otherwise → ZustandForm
```

Form sections live in `config.tsx`. Dropdowns are `type: 'relationship'`; there is
no `'select'`. See [Forms & fields](/docs/patterns/form-pattern) and
[ZustandForm](/docs/components/zustand-form).

## Field type

```
What does the field hold?
├─ One value from a list (dropdown) → 'relationship', options from loadField
├─ Several values from a list → 'multiselect', options from loadField
├─ A list of child records edited inline → 'crud'
├─ Money → 'currency'
├─ A date, with or without typing a mask → 'date' / 'masked-date'
├─ Text with a fixed format (phone, document number) → 'masked'
└─ Anything custom → 'component'
```

Every type, with its props: [Field types](/docs/reference/field-types). Nested
records: [Nested data](/docs/patterns/nested-data) and [CRUD field](/docs/patterns/crud-field).

## Detail component

```
Showing one record?
├─ Page shell (dedicated page only) → DetailLayout
├─ Grouping fields → DetailCard
├─ Label + value → DetailField
├─ Metrics in a grid → DetailStatsGrid
├─ Status badge → DetailStatus
├─ Warning or info block → DetailAlert
├─ Avatar or photo → DetailAvatar
├─ Action buttons → DetailActions
└─ Sections inside the view dialog → ContentTabs
```

See [Detail views](/docs/patterns/detail-page).

## List

```
Listing records?
├─ A CrudConfig module → ListPage (search, sorting, filters, export, row actions, dialogs)
├─ A list inside a tab of a hub page → ListPage with embedded
└─ A table that is not a CRUD module and needs full control → DataTable
```

See [List pages](/docs/patterns/listpage-pattern) and [DataTable](/docs/components/data-table).

## Data layer

```
Fetching or mutating data?
├─ In a CrudConfig module → config.query.queryFn + config.mutations.*.mutationFn
│  · queryFn resolves PaginatedResponse<T>
│  · mutationFn resolves { success, data? }
│  · only lib/api/<module>-client.ts calls fetch()
└─ Outside a CrudConfig → your own React Query hook, imported from @tanstack/react-query
```

See [Data layer](/docs/patterns/react-query).

## Layout

```
What are you laying out?
│
├─ The app shell (sidebar, header, breadcrumb, Cmd+K) → AdminShell
│
├─ A page with several views (hub)
│  ├─ Up to 5 tabs → ShellPage + AdminHeader + AdminTabs + useTabUrlSync
│  └─ 6+ sections → AdminPortal
│
├─ A page with one view → ShellPage + AdminHeader + ShellContent
│
└─ A shell AdminShell cannot express → AppShell (lower-level primitive)
```

See [App shell & providers](/docs/patterns/provider-setup), [AdminShell](/docs/components/admin-shell)
and [ShellPage](/docs/components/shell-page).

## Chart

```
Showing a chart?
├─ In a dashboard card with title and actions → ChartWidget (line, bar, pie)
├─ In your own layout → LineChart / BarChart / AreaChart / PieChart
├─ A donut → PieChart with innerRadius > 0
└─ Radar, bars + line, scatter, funnel... → Recharts directly
```

See [ChartWidget](/docs/components/chart-widget) and [Dashboards](/docs/patterns/dashboard).

---

# Troubleshooting

> Two copies of a peer dependency, "No QueryClient set", consuming the packages via link:, NestJS guard exceptions across package instances, and the Zustand getSnapshot loop

Source: apps/docs/content/docs/troubleshooting.mdx

Most hard-to-read errors in a TelamonJS app have one of two causes: **two copies of a peer
dependency** in the same process, or a **dynamic Zustand selector** inside a custom hook. This page
covers both. Problems specific to one feature stay on that feature's page: see the Troubleshooting
sections of [Auth](/docs/packages/auth#troubleshooting) and
[Provider Setup](/docs/patterns/provider-setup#troubleshooting).

---

## Two copies of a peer dependency

`@tanstack/react-query`, `react`, `next-intl` and, on the API side, `@nestjs/common` are **peer
dependencies** of the TelamonJS packages. When you install a package from the registry, its peers
resolve to the app's own copy, so there is one instance of each.

That stops being true when the package is **linked** instead of installed (`link:` or `file:` in
`package.json`, `pnpm link`, or a local checkout outside the app's workspace). The linked package
then resolves its peers (and its own dependencies, such as `lucide-react`) from **its own**
`node_modules`, and the process ends up with two copies of the same module. Anything that relies on
module identity breaks:

| Peer | What breaks |
| --- | --- |
| `@tanstack/react-query` | React context: `No QueryClient set`, or `query.isFetched is not a function` |
| `lucide-react` | Types: a `LucideIcon` from the app is not assignable to the library's |
| `@nestjs/common` | `instanceof`: a guard's `UnauthorizedException` becomes a 500 |

The fix in every case is to end up with a single copy. The sections below give the specific
setting for each peer.

---

## "No QueryClient set"

**Symptom:** React Query hooks throw `No QueryClient set, use QueryClientProvider to set one`,
even though a provider is mounted.

**Cause:** two instances of the react-query module. The provider registers its context on one
instance and the hook reads the other.

**Fix:**

1. Import `QueryClient`, `QueryCache`, `MutationCache`, `useQuery` and the rest directly from
   `@tanstack/react-query`. `@telamonjs/ui` deliberately does **not** re-export them: a re-export
   creates a second instance under `optimizePackageImports`.
2. Let Next.js optimize the barrel instead of using deep imports:

   ```js title="next.config.js"
   experimental: {
     optimizePackageImports: ['@telamonjs/ui', 'lucide-react'],
   }
   ```

   Apps generated by the CLI already ship this setting.
3. Create **one** `QueryClient` per app (in `useState`, in a client component) and pass it both to
   your own `QueryClientProvider` and to `AppProviders` in `config.queryClient`. The complete
   providers file is in [Provider Setup](/docs/patterns/provider-setup#2-the-apps-queryclient).

`next-intl` follows the same rule as react-query: it is not re-exported either, so import
`useTranslations` and friends from `next-intl` directly.

### When the app's client comes from another copy

With a linked `@telamonjs/ui`, the app's `QueryClient` can come from a different copy (sometimes a
different version) of react-query. A foreign client breaks the library's observers
(`query.isFetched is not a function`), so `AppProviders` ignores it, logs a development-only warning
and falls back to its internal client:

```text
[telamonjs] config.queryClient comes from another @tanstack/react-query copy (link mode?) — using the internal client.
```

This is why the providers file keeps its own `QueryClientProvider` around `AppProviders`, with the
**same** client: in that situation the outer provider is the one serving the app's hooks. With the
package installed from the registry there is a single copy, and `AppProviders` uses the app's
client for the whole tree.

The warning also explains a confusing difference between environments. If the app passes its
client **only** to an outer `QueryClientProvider` and not to `AppProviders`, its global `onError`
handlers work in linked development (two copies, two clients) and silently stop working with the
published package (one copy, where the client `AppProviders` creates shadows the app's).

---

## Consuming the packages via `link:`

Linking a local TelamonJS checkout into an app is useful to test a change before it is published.
Keep these rules in mind:

- **Build first.** The packages resolve types and code from `dist/`. Run `pnpm build` in the
  TelamonJS checkout before starting the app, and keep `pnpm dev` running in the package you are
  changing. Without a build the app fails with `Cannot find module '@telamonjs/…'`, which is the
  missing build, not a broken import.
- **Prefer an injected `file:` dependency over `link:`.** With a plain `link:`, `@telamonjs/ui`
  resolves its peers (`next-intl`, `@tanstack/react-query`, `next-auth`, `next-themes`) from the
  checkout's own `node_modules`, so the app ends up with two copies and errors like *"context from
  NextIntlClientProvider was not found"*. With pnpm, point the app at the checkout with
  `file:` and mark it injected, so the package is copied into the app and resolves the app's peers:

  ```json title="package.json"
  {
    "dependencies": { "@telamonjs/ui": "file:../telamonjs/packages/ui" },
    "dependenciesMeta": { "@telamonjs/ui": { "injected": true } },
    "pnpm": {
      "overrides": {
        "@telamonjs/data": "link:../telamonjs/packages/data",
        "@telamonjs/logger": "link:../telamonjs/packages/logger"
      }
    }
  }
  ```

  `telamonjs link` writes exactly these entries and `telamonjs unlink` removes them (see
  [CLI › link / unlink](/docs/packages/cli#link--unlink)).

  Re-run `pnpm install` after rebuilding the package so the injected copy picks up the new `dist/`.
  The overrides are required, not optional: in the checkout, `@telamonjs/ui` declares
  `@telamonjs/logger` and `@telamonjs/data` as `workspace:^`, which only resolves through an
  override (without one, `pnpm install` fails with `ERR_PNPM_WORKSPACE_PKG_NOT_FOUND`). Run
  `telamonjs unlink` before committing or building against the registry; monorepos generated
  by the CLI do it in a pre-commit hook.
- **One copy of each peer.** Expect the two-copy problems above. Keep the
  `optimizePackageImports` setting, pass the app's client to `AppProviders`, and keep the outer
  `QueryClientProvider`.
- **Menu icons as strings.** Pass `icon: 'Receipt'`, not the Lucide component: with two copies of
  `lucide-react`, the app's `LucideIcon` is a different type from the library's and type-check
  fails. Strings are resolved through `setIconResolver()` and work the same in both setups (see
  [Icon Resolver](/docs/patterns/provider-setup#icon-resolver-seticonresolver)).
- **Switch back before shipping.** None of the workarounds on this page are needed with a
  registry install, and some of them (the outer provider) are harmless there. Test the final
  version against the published package.

---

## NestJS guard exceptions across package instances

**Symptom:** a request with a missing or invalid token (or without the permission) gets a **500**
instead of a **401** (or **403**), but only in development.

**Cause:** with `@telamonjs/auth` or `@telamonjs/permissions` linked, the guard and the host API
resolve `@nestjs/common` from different `node_modules`, so there are two `UnauthorizedException`
(and `ForbiddenException`) classes. Nest's exception filters use `instanceof`, so the exception
thrown by the package's copy is not recognized by the host's filters and surfaces as a generic 500.

**Fix:** with a registry install there is nothing to do: `@nestjs/common` is a peer dependency and
resolves to the host's single copy. While the package is linked, pass `createException` to both
guards so they throw the host's own classes. Both options share one signature, so one function
serves both:

```ts title="src/common/guards/http-exception.ts"
import { ForbiddenException, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common' // the host's copy

export const createException = (status: 401 | 403, message: string) =>
  status === 401 ? new UnauthorizedException(message) : new ForbiddenException(message)
```

```ts
export const JwtAuthGuard = createJwtAuthGuard({ createException })
export const PermissionsGuard = createPermissionsGuard({ createException })
```

Without the option, the guards keep throwing the package's own Nest exceptions.

`@telamonjs/queue/nestjs` also takes `@nestjs/common` as a peer and has no such option: while it is
linked, catch its exceptions in the host and re-throw them with the host's classes (match on
`e.name`, since `instanceof` is what fails).

---

## Zustand: "The result of getSnapshot should be cached"

**Symptom:** React logs `The result of getSnapshot should be cached to avoid an infinite loop`, and
the component re-renders until React gives up. The stack trace goes through
`useSyncExternalStore` and Zustand's `useStore`.

**Cause:** a **dynamic selector** (one that depends on a hook parameter, such as
`state => state.forms[formId]`) inside a custom hook. The selector is recreated on every render.
Wrapping it in `useCallback`, `useMemo` or a ref does not fix it.

**Fix:** subscribe to the store and select locally:

```ts
// ❌ inside a custom hook
const data = useFormStore(state => state.forms[formId])

// ✅
const formState = useFormStore()
const data = formState.forms[formId]
```

Static selectors (`state => state.items`) are fine. The full explanation, the trade-offs and when
to reach for `useShallow` are in [Zustand Selector Pattern](/docs/patterns/zustand-selector).

---

# Zustand Selector Pattern

> Avoid infinite loops - the getSnapshot should be cached warning

Source: apps/docs/content/docs/patterns/zustand-selector.mdx

How to avoid the React warning `The result of getSnapshot should be cached to avoid an infinite loop` when using Zustand in custom hooks.

<Callout type='error' title='Critical'>
  Dynamic selectors inside custom hooks cause **infinite loops** in React. This
  pattern is mandatory when writing hooks around Zustand stores.
</Callout>

---

## The Problem

Using dynamic selectors (selectors that depend on hook parameters) inside custom hooks recreates the selector on every render:

```typescript
// ❌ WRONG - dynamic selectors cause infinite loops
export const useForm = (formId: string) => {
  // Selector is recreated on every render
  const data = useFormStore((state) => state.forms[formId])
  const meta = useFormStore((state) => state.formMeta[formId])

  return { data, meta }
}
```

### Attempts That Do NOT Work

```typescript
// ❌ useCallback does not fix it (mutable deps recreate the function)
const data = useFormStore(
  React.useCallback((state) => state.forms[formId], [formId])
)

// ❌ useMemo does not fix it either
const selectData = React.useMemo(() => (state) => state.forms[formId], [formId])
const data = useFormStore(selectData)

// ❌ useRef with useEffect causes race conditions
const selectorRef = React.useRef((state) => state.forms[formId])
React.useEffect(() => {
  selectorRef.current = (state) => state.forms[formId]
}, [formId])
const data = useFormStore(selectorRef.current)
```

---

## The Solution

**Subscribe to the entire store and select in the component:**

```typescript
export const useForm = (formId: string) => {
  // ✅ CORRECT - subscribe to the whole store (stable reference)
  const formState = useFormStore()

  // ✅ Selection happens in the component (not in the selector)
  const data = formState.forms[formId] || {}
  const meta = formState.formMeta[formId] || defaultMeta
  const isValid = formState.isFormValid(formId)

  return { data, meta, isValid }
}
```

---

## Golden Rules

### 1. NEVER use dynamic selectors in custom hooks

```typescript
// ❌ DON'T
const useMyHook = (id: string) => {
  return useStore((state) => state.items[id])
}

// ✅ DO
const useMyHook = (id: string) => {
  const store = useStore()
  return store.items[id]
}
```

### 2. Static selectors are OK

```typescript
// ✅ OK - selector does not depend on props/state
const allItems = useStore((state) => state.items)
const count = useStore((state) => state.count)
```

### 3. Prefer full subscription in custom hooks

```typescript
// ✅ Best approach for custom hooks
const useFormData = (formId: string) => {
  const store = useFormStore() // subscribe to whole store
  return store.forms[formId] // select locally
}
```

---

## Trade-offs

**Full subscription advantages:** zero warnings, simple and predictable code, no race conditions, works every time.

**Disadvantages:** re-renders on ANY store change (not just the selected slice), less optimized for large stores.

### When is that OK?

- Small/medium stores
- Specific custom hooks (e.g. `useForm(id)`)
- When simplicity beats micro-optimization

### When to optimize

If the store is very large and there are measurable performance issues:

```typescript
import { useShallow } from 'zustand/react/shallow'

const { data, meta } = useFormStore(
  useShallow((state) => ({
    data: state.forms[formId],
    meta: state.formMeta[formId],
  }))
)
```

<Callout type='warn'>
  `useShallow` can still have edge cases. Prefer full subscription.
</Callout>

---

## How to Identify the Problem

1. **Console warning:** `The result of getSnapshot should be cached to avoid an infinite loop`
2. **Stack trace shows Zustand:** `useSyncExternalStore` → `useStore (zustand)` → your hook
3. **Code uses a dynamic selector in a hook:** grep for `useStore(state => state.items[id])`-style calls inside parameterized hooks

## Checklist

- Does the hook receive dynamic parameters (id, formId, etc.)?
- Does it use `useStore(selector)` with those parameters?
- If YES → refactor to full subscription
- If NO → static selector is fine
- Test in the browser and verify the console has no warnings

If there are too many re-renders afterwards: memoize consumer components with `React.memo`, split the store into sub-stores, or use `useShallow` as a last resort.

---

## Related

- [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) — this and the other hard-to-read runtime errors
- [Provider Setup](/docs/patterns/provider-setup) — store/provider hierarchy
- [useTableState](/docs/hooks/use-table-state) — table state without hand-rolled selectors

---

# Bulk Operations

> Efficiently add, remove, retry, clean and drain many jobs at once

Source: apps/docs/content/docs/queue/bulk-operations.mdx

Individual job operations are simple but inefficient at scale — adding 1,000 jobs in
a loop means 1,000 Redis round-trips. Bulk operations do the same work in far fewer
calls: `addBulk` sends the whole list in one BullMQ `addBulk`, and removals and
retries run in batches of 100. That is much faster and much lighter on Redis.

```typescript
// ❌ 1000 Redis calls
for (const data of dataArray) {
  await queueManager.add(SendEmailJob, data)
}

// ✅ 1 bulk call
await queueManager.addBulk(
  SendEmailJob,
  dataArray.map(data => ({ data }))
)
```

## Available operations

| Operation    | Queue-level                    | QueueManager-level                                      |
| ------------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Add          | `queue.addBulk()`              | `queueManager.addBulk(JobClass, entries, defaults?)`    |
| Remove       | `queue.removeBulk(ids)`        | `queueManager.removeBulk(queueName, ids)`               |
| Retry        | `queue.retryBulk(ids?)`        | `queueManager.retryBulk(queueName, ids?)`               |
| Retry all    | —                              | `queueManager.retryAllFailed(options?)`                 |
| Clean        | —                              | `queueManager.cleanQueue(...)` / `cleanAll(...)`        |
| Drain        | `queue.drain()`                | `queueManager.drainQueue(name)` / `drainAll()`          |
| Pause/Resume | —                              | `pauseQueues(names)` / `resumeQueues(names)` / `pauseAll()` / `resumeAll()` |

## addBulk

Type-safe bulk add through the `QueueManager`, with shared defaults and per-job
overrides:

```typescript
import { QueueManager, JobPriority } from '@telamonjs/queue'

await queueManager.addBulk(
  SendEmailJob,
  [
    {
      data: { to: 'vip@example.com', subject: 'Welcome!' },
      opts: { priority: JobPriority.CRITICAL }, // per-job override
    },
    { data: { to: 'regular@example.com', subject: 'Welcome!' } },
  ],
  {
    priority: JobPriority.HIGH, // default for all entries
    attempts: 5,
    backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 5000 },
  }
)
```

For very large datasets (> 10,000 jobs), split into chunks of ~500–1,000 to keep
memory bounded:

```typescript
const chunkSize = 1000
for (let i = 0; i < emails.length; i += chunkSize) {
  const chunk = emails.slice(i, i + chunkSize)
  await queueManager.addBulk(SendEmailJob, chunk.map(email => ({ data: email })))
}
```

## removeBulk

```typescript
const removed = await queueManager.removeBulk('send-email', ['job-id-1', 'job-id-2'])
```

Processes in batches of 100, handles non-existent IDs gracefully and returns the
count of successfully removed jobs — compare it with the requested count to detect
partial removals.

## retryBulk / retryAllFailed

```typescript
// Retry specific failed jobs in one queue
await queueManager.retryBulk('send-email', ['job-1', 'job-2'])

// Retry ALL failed jobs in one queue
await queueManager.retryBulk('send-email')

// Retry ALL failed jobs across ALL queues
const results = await queueManager.retryAllFailed()
// { 'send-email': 5, 'generate-report': 2 }

// With option overrides
await queueManager.retryAllFailed({ attempts: 10 })
```

## cleanQueue / cleanAll

Clean old jobs to prevent Redis bloat:

```typescript
// Completed jobs older than 24h, up to 1000 jobs, from one queue
const cleaned = await queueManager.cleanQueue('send-email', 86400000, 1000, 'completed')

// From all queues
const results = await queueManager.cleanAll(86400000, 1000, 'completed')
// { 'send-email': ['id1', 'id2'], 'generate-report': ['id3'] }
```

Run this periodically (e.g. a daily scheduled job cleaning jobs older than 7 days).

## drain — graceful shutdown

`drain()` pauses the queue, so workers stop picking up new jobs, then waits (up to
60 seconds) for the **active** jobs to finish. Waiting and delayed jobs are not
processed: they stay in Redis and run after the queue is resumed. It resolves with
the number of jobs that finished while it waited.

```typescript
async function gracefulShutdown() {
  await queueManager.drainAll() // stop taking jobs, let active ones finish
  await queueManager.close() // close all connections
  process.exit(0)
}

process.on('SIGTERM', gracefulShutdown)
process.on('SIGINT', gracefulShutdown)
```

<Callout type='warn' title='Resume after a deploy'>
  A drained queue stays paused in Redis. The next worker process must resume it
  (`queueManager.resumeQueues(names)`) or nothing in that queue runs again.
</Callout>

## Pause / Resume

```typescript
// Specific queues
await queueManager.pauseQueues(['send-email', 'generate-report'])
await queueManager.resumeQueues(['send-email', 'generate-report'])

// All workers (maintenance mode)
await queueManager.pauseAll()
await queueManager.resumeAll()
```

## Example: maintenance mode

```typescript
async function enterMaintenanceMode() {
  await queueManager.pauseAll()

  // Wait for active jobs, then verify
  const stats = await queueManager.getStats()
  const activeJobs = Object.values(stats).reduce((sum, s) => sum + s.active, 0)
  if (activeJobs > 0) console.warn(`Still ${activeJobs} active jobs`)
}

async function exitMaintenanceMode() {
  await queueManager.resumeAll()
}
```

## Related

- [Error Handling](/docs/queue/error-handling)
- [Dead Letter Queue](/docs/queue/dead-letter-queue)
- [Priorities](/docs/queue/priorities)

# Dashboard

> The Jobs Dashboard — real-time queue monitoring UI from @telamonjs/ui/queue, plus the embeddable Bull Board server

Source: apps/docs/content/docs/queue/dashboard.mdx

The **Jobs Dashboard** is a complete React monitoring UI for BullMQ queues, shipped
in the `@telamonjs/ui/queue` subpath. It talks to your backend through a
pluggable **adapter** (NestJS, Next.js or custom) and uses React Query for data
fetching plus **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** for real-time updates.

Features:

- **Real time** — live queue stats, job event timeline (started / completed /
  failed / progress / retrying) over SSE with automatic reconnection and graceful
  degradation to polling when SSE is unavailable
- **History** — completed/failed job history across all queues with search, date
  range filters and aggregate stats
- **Queue actions** — pause, resume, clean, retry-all, drain; per-job retry,
  remove, promote; bulk retry/remove; manual job dispatch
- **Job configuration** — enable/disable jobs (per job or per module), edit cron
  pattern, priority, concurrency and timeout at runtime, with a change history
  audit trail
- **Redis metrics** — connection utilization and health

## Mounting in your app

The plug-and-play entry point is `QueueTabbedDashboard` — a shell page with four
lazy-loaded tabs (`tempo-real`, `configuracao`, `redis`, `historico`) built on the
canonical TelamonJS shell (`ShellPage` + `AdminHeader` + `AdminTabs`).

```tsx title="app/admin/jobs/page.tsx"
'use client'

import {
  QueueTabbedDashboard,
  QueueApiProvider,
  createNestJSAdapter,
} from '@telamonjs/ui/queue'

const adapter = createNestJSAdapter({
  baseUrl: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL!,
  getAuthToken: async () => {
    const session = await getSession()
    return session?.user?.accessToken ?? null
  },
})

export default function JobsPage() {
  return (
    <QueueApiProvider adapter={adapter}>
      <QueueTabbedDashboard syncTabWithUrl />
    </QueueApiProvider>
  )
}
```

<Callout type='info' title='Auto-provider'>
  If no `QueueApiProvider` is present, `QueueTabbedDashboard` creates a NestJS
  adapter automatically from `apiUrl` (default:
  `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`, falling back to relative URLs). Wrapping it
  explicitly is only needed for custom adapters or auth logic.
</Callout>

### QueueTabbedDashboard props

| Prop             | Type                       | Default                             |
| ---------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `initialTab`     | `'tempo-real' \| 'configuracao' \| 'redis' \| 'historico'` | `'tempo-real'` |
| `tabs`           | subset of the four tab ids | all four                            |
| `title`          | `string`                   | `'Central de Jobs'`                 |
| `description`    | `string`                   | queue monitoring subtitle           |
| `icon`           | `ComponentType`            | —                                   |
| `moduleIcons`    | `Record<string, ReactNode \| IconComponent>` | — (module group icons: emoji, node or icon component) |
| `moduleLabels`   | `Record<string, I18nText>` | — (module group titles; key order = group order) |
| `jobLabel`       | `(jobName: string) => I18nText \| undefined` | — (job label override) |
| `enableSSE`      | `boolean`                  | `true`                              |
| `pollInterval`   | `number` (ms)              | `2000` (timeline polling while SSE is down) |
| `syncTabWithUrl` | `boolean`                  | `false` (reads/writes `?tab=` param)|
| `onTabChange`    | `(tab: string) => void`    | —                                   |
| `apiUrl`         | `string`                   | `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`   |

### Module and job labels

Jobs are grouped by **module**, the prefix of the job name (`comunicacoes_enviar-email`
belongs to `comunicacoes`). Module keys and job names are Redis keys, so they cannot
carry accents or spaces. Three props turn them into real names:

- `moduleLabels` sets the group titles in the Real-time and Configuration tabs. Its key
  order is also the group order in both tabs. Modules it does not list follow,
  alphabetically by label. Without it, groups show the raw key, capitalized, in
  alphabetical order.
- Job labels follow one precedence, first match wins:
  1. `jobLabel(jobName)`, when it returns something other than `undefined`;
  2. the job contract's `displayName`, which `@telamonjs/queue` serves as the contract's
     short `label`, else its `description`;
  3. the formatted job name: the module prefix is removed and the words are capitalized,
     so `comunicacoes_enviar-email` becomes "Enviar Email".

  Set `label` on the contract to keep long `description` sentences out of the rows. The
  label is used in queue rows, timeline and history rows, job details, modal titles and
  the `JobDetailPage` title, which also shows the contract's `description` below it.
- `moduleIcons` takes an emoji, any React node, or an icon component such as a Lucide icon.

Text values are `I18nText`: a literal, or `msg('key')` resolved in the active locale.

```tsx title="app/admin/jobs/jobs-dashboard.tsx"
'use client'

import { Mail, Wrench } from 'lucide-react'
import { msg } from '@telamonjs/ui'
import { QueueTabbedDashboard } from '@telamonjs/ui/queue'

const moduleLabels = {
  comunicacoes: 'Comunicações',
  manutencao: msg('jobs.modules.maintenance'),
}
const moduleIcons = { comunicacoes: Mail, manutencao: Wrench }
const jobLabels: Record<string, string> = {
  'manutencao_limpar-audit-logs': 'Limpar logs de auditoria',
}

export function JobsDashboard() {
  return (
    <QueueTabbedDashboard
      moduleLabels={moduleLabels}
      moduleIcons={moduleIcons}
      jobLabel={name => jobLabels[name]}
    />
  )
}
```

<Callout type='warn' title='Functions do not cross the server boundary'>
  `jobLabel` and icon components are functions, so a Server Component cannot pass them to
  `QueueTabbedDashboard`. Set them in a Client Component, as above.
</Callout>

## Adapters

An adapter implements the `QueueApiAdapter` interface (or the superset
`QueueConfigApiAdapter`, which adds job configuration and SSE methods). Two
factories ship with the package:

<Tabs items={['NestJS', 'Next.js', 'Custom']}>
<Tab value='NestJS'>

For a separate NestJS REST API. Supports Bearer token and cookie auth, custom
headers and a custom response parser (e.g. SuperJSON):

```typescript
import { createNestJSAdapter } from '@telamonjs/ui/queue'

const adapter = createNestJSAdapter({
  baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com', // endpoints prefixed with /v1
  getAuthToken: async () => token, // optional Bearer token
  headers: { 'X-Custom': 'value' }, // optional
  parseResponse: async res => res.json(), // optional (default)
})
```

</Tab>
<Tab value='Next.js'>

For queue endpoints hosted in the same Next.js app (API routes):

```typescript
import { createNextJSAdapter } from '@telamonjs/ui/queue'

const adapter = createNextJSAdapter({
  /* NextJSAdapterConfig */
})
```

</Tab>
<Tab value='Custom'>

Implement the interface directly for any backend:

```typescript
import type { QueueConfigApiAdapter } from '@telamonjs/ui/queue'

const adapter: QueueConfigApiAdapter = {
  getStats: async () => fetchMyBackend('/queue/stats'),
  // ... remaining methods
}
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Expected server contract

The dashboard is backend-agnostic — whatever the adapter resolves is what renders.
The reference NestJS backend exposes this REST surface (all under `/v1`):

| Method   | Endpoint                                  | Purpose                                        |
| -------- | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `GET`    | `/v1/queue/stats`                         | `DashboardStats` — totals + per-queue stats    |
| `GET`    | `/v1/admin/metrics/redis`                 | Redis connection metrics                       |
| `GET`    | `/v1/queue/jobs?queue&state&limit`        | Jobs of one queue/state                        |
| `GET`    | `/v1/queue/jobs/all?status&queue&search&limit&offset` | Jobs across all queues, filtered   |
| `GET`    | `/v1/queue/history?queue&limit`           | History of one queue                           |
| `GET`    | `/v1/queue/history/all?statuses&queue&search&startDate&endDate&limit&offset` | Global history + aggregate stats |
| `POST`   | `/v1/queue/actions`                       | `{ type, queueName, status? }` — pause/resume/clean/retry-all/drain |
| `POST`   | `/v1/queue/jobs/retry` / `remove` / `promote` | `{ queueName, jobId }` single-job actions  |
| `POST`   | `/v1/queue/jobs/bulk`                     | `{ queueName, jobIds, operation }` bulk retry/remove |
| `GET`    | `/v1/queue/dispatch`                      | List manually dispatchable jobs                |
| `POST`   | `/v1/queue/dispatch`                      | `{ queueName, data }` — dispatch a job         |
| `GET`    | `/v1/queue/config`                        | All job configurations                         |
| `GET/PATCH` | `/v1/queue/config/:jobName`            | Read / update one job config                   |
| `POST`   | `/v1/queue/config/:jobName/toggle`        | Enable/disable a job                           |
| `POST`   | `/v1/queue/config/modules/:module/toggle` | Enable/disable all jobs of a module            |
| `GET`    | `/v1/queue/config/:jobName/history`       | Config change audit trail                      |
| `GET`    | `/v1/queue/events`                        | **SSE stream** (stats + job events)            |

Contract notes (enforced by the reference backend and reflected in the adapter
types):

- `queueName: '*'` (all queues) is only accepted with `type: 'clean'` — any other
  action targeting `'*'` returns 400.
- `startDate`/`endDate` are ISO 8601 strings; unparseable dates return 400.
- `limit` must be an integer from 1 to 500 and `offset` an integer `>= 0`;
  `state`/`status` must be a known job state (`statuses` on `history/all`:
  `completed`/`failed`). Anything else returns 400.
- `PATCH /config/:jobName` and `POST /config/:jobName/toggle` return 404 for a job
  with no stored config. The PATCH body is validated (`cronPattern` a valid cron
  pattern, `priority` an integer from 1 to 10, `concurrency`/`timeout` positive
  integers, `null` clears a field) and the toggles require a boolean `enabled`;
  invalid input returns 400.
- History/jobs responses may set `approximate: true` when `total` is a
  post-filter count (active search/date filters).
- The SSE endpoint requires the `jobs.execute` permission in the reference
  backend — the connection is rejected otherwise.

### Protecting the routes

`QueueHttpModule.forRoot()` (from `@telamonjs/queue/nestjs`) declares no
permission on its routes unless you ask it to. With the usual global auth and
permissions guards, that means every logged-in user can dispatch jobs, remove
them and edit job configs. Set both options:

```ts
QueueHttpModule.forRoot({
  depsFactory: () => ({ queues, jobConfigStore, contracts, eventBroadcaster }),
  getActor: req => req.user.email,
  readPermission: 'queue.read',   // every GET route, the SSE stream included
  writePermission: 'queue.write', // every POST/PATCH route
})
```

Each option takes what `@Permissions(...)` from
[`@telamonjs/permissions`](/docs/packages/permissions) takes: a string, or a
list of clauses (OR between entries, an inner array is AND). They are written as
the metadata that package's guard reads, so that guard (global, or in `guards`)
is what enforces them.

Guards run once per request, and the SSE stream is one long request. The route
ends each stream after `sseMaxAgeMs` (a `forRoot()` option, 5 minutes by
default) and the dashboard reconnects through your guards, so an expired token,
a revoked session or a removed `readPermission` stops the feed within that time.
The stream's last frame is `event: reconnect`, so the dashboard reconnects at
once and keeps showing `connected`.

## Real-time updates (SSE)

With `enableSSE` (the default), the dashboard connects to the adapter's
`getSSEConfig()` URL and feeds the React Query cache:

- **Stats updates** pushed by the server (~5s cadence) refresh the queue cards
- **Job events** (`job:started`, `job:completed`, `job:failed`, `job:progress`,
  `job:retrying`) update the live timeline in real time
- Rapid event bursts are debounced into a single stats refetch
- Automatic reconnection with status reporting
  (`connecting | connected | disconnected | error`)
- If the adapter does not implement `getSSEConfig()`, the dashboard falls back to
  React Query polling
- The live timeline polls every `pollInterval` only while SSE is down; with the stream
  connected it polls every 30s as a safety net, and not at all while another tab is open

## Other components

The tabs, modals, tables and data hooks inside the dashboard are internal. Besides
`QueueTabbedDashboard`, the subpath exports two more ready-made screens (both under the same
`QueueApiProvider`):

```tsx
import { QueueDashboard, JobDetailPage } from '@telamonjs/ui/queue'

// Single-page (non-tabbed) dashboard: stats cards + per-queue table with actions
<QueueDashboard pollInterval={10000} showHeader settingsHref='/admin/jobs/config' />

// Configuration + change history of one job (fetched through the adapter)
<JobDetailPage jobName='send-email' backHref='/admin/jobs' onRefresh={() => router.refresh()} />
```

| `JobDetailPage` prop | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jobName` | `string` | Job whose config and history are fetched |
| `apiUrl` | `string` | API URL override (default: env var) |
| `config` / `history` | `JobConfig` / `JobHistoryEntry[]` | Pre-fetched data; skips the fetch |
| `backHref` / `onBack` | `string` / `() => void` | Back navigation |
| `onRefresh` | `() => void` | Called after a successful update |
| `moduleLabels` / `jobLabel` | as on `QueueTabbedDashboard` | Module badge and title; pass the dashboard's values |

The header `QueueDashboard` renders with `showHeader` is exported as `QueueDashboardHeader`, and
the display config of a job state (icon, label, colors) as the type `JobStatusConfig`:

```tsx
import { QueueDashboardHeader, type JobStatusConfig } from '@telamonjs/ui/queue'
```

<Callout type='warn'>
The older names `DashboardHeader` and `StatusConfig` are still exported from
`@telamonjs/ui/queue` but deprecated: the root barrel has a `DashboardHeader` (the
`DashboardShell` header) and a `StatusConfig` (the `DetailStatus` config) that are different
symbols.
</Callout>

Types (`QueueStats`, `DashboardStats`, `JobInfo`, `JobConfig`, `JobHistoryEntry`,
`QueueApiAdapter`, `QueueConfigApiAdapter`, …) are exported from the same subpath.

## Bull Board (server-side dashboard)

Independently of the React dashboard, `@telamonjs/queue/dashboard`
ships an embeddable **Bull Board** UI for low-level queue inspection:

```typescript
import { startDashboard } from '@telamonjs/queue/dashboard'

// Standalone Express server (default port 3005)
const dashboard = startDashboard({
  port: 3005,
  queueManager,
  auth: {
    enabled: true,
    username: 'admin',
    password: process.env.DASHBOARD_PASSWORD!,
  },
})

// The app owns shutdown: startDashboard installs no signal handlers
process.on('SIGTERM', () => dashboard.server.close())
```

`startDashboard` returns the Express app with the listening HTTP `server`
attached, and also exposes a `/health` endpoint listing registered queues.

Or mount it into an existing Express app:

```typescript
import { createDashboardRouter } from '@telamonjs/queue/dashboard'

const app = express()
app.use(
  '/admin/queue',
  createDashboardRouter({
    queueManager,
    auth: { enabled: true, username: 'admin', password: process.env.DASHBOARD_PASSWORD! },
  })
)
```

Express 4 and 5 are both supported, so the router mounts into a Nest 11 app's
Express 5 as well.

Basic-auth protection is opt-in via the `auth` config, and both functions honor
it — always enable it outside local development. `auth.enabled: true` with a
missing or empty `username` or `password` throws a `ConfigurationError` at
startup instead of serving the board unprotected.

# Dead Letter Queue

> Inspect, analyze and manually retry jobs that permanently failed after exhausting retries

Source: apps/docs/content/docs/queue/dead-letter-queue.mdx

When a job fails repeatedly and exhausts all retry attempts
(`attemptsMade >= attempts`), instead of being lost it is automatically moved to the
**Dead Letter Queue**, preserving the job data, error details (message, stack, code),
attempt count and failure timestamp. From there you can inspect, analyze failure
patterns, retry after fixing the root cause, or delete.

- **Retry** (automatic, with backoff) handles *transient* failures.
- **DLQ** (manual) handles *permanent* failures that need investigation first.

## Enable / disable

DLQ is **enabled by default**:

```typescript
import { QueueManager } from '@telamonjs/queue'

const queueManager = new QueueManager({
  redis: { host: 'localhost', port: 6379 },
  enableDLQ: true, // default
})
```

All jobs share a single DLQ per `QueueManager`, named `{prefix}-dlq`
(e.g. prefix `production` → queue `production-dlq`). Entries are persisted in Redis
and survive restarts.

## Operations

```typescript
const dlq = queueManager.getDLQ()
if (!dlq) return // DLQ disabled

// List (with pagination)
const all = await dlq.list()
const firstPage = await dlq.list(0, 9)

// Get one entry
const entry = await dlq.get('dlq-send-email-job-123')
// entry: { id, jobName, originalJobId, data, error: { message, stack, code },
//          attempts, failedAt }

// Statistics
const stats = await dlq.getStats()
// { total: 47,
//   byJobName: { 'send-email': 23, 'process-payment': 15, 'generate-report': 9 },
//   oldest: Date, newest: Date }

// Filter by job type
const failedEmails = await dlq.filterByJobName('send-email')

// Delete one / clear all
await dlq.delete('dlq-send-email-job-123')
const cleared = await dlq.clear() // ⚠️ irreversible
```

### Retry a failed job

```typescript
const dlq = queueManager.getDLQ()
const queue = queueManager.getQueue('send-email')

if (dlq && queue) {
  const success = await dlq.retry('dlq-send-email-job-123', queue.getRawQueue())
}
```

On retry, the job is re-added to its original queue with reset attempts and removed
from the DLQ — a worker picks it up and processes it normally.

## Best practices

### Monitor DLQ size

```typescript
setInterval(async () => {
  const dlq = queueManager.getDLQ()
  if (!dlq) return

  const stats = await dlq.getStats()
  if (stats.total > 100) {
    await sendAlert(`DLQ has ${stats.total} failed jobs!`)
  }
}, 60000)
```

### Investigate before retrying

```typescript
async function investigateAndRetry(dlqEntryId: string) {
  const dlq = queueManager.getDLQ()
  if (!dlq) return

  const entry = await dlq.get(dlqEntryId)
  if (!entry) return

  logger.warn('Failed job investigation', {
    jobName: entry.jobName,
    error: entry.error.message,
    attempts: entry.attempts,
  })

  const isFixed = await checkIfIssueIsFixed(entry.error.code)
  if (isFixed) {
    const queue = queueManager.getQueue(entry.jobName)
    if (queue) await dlq.retry(entry.id, queue.getRawQueue())
  }
}
```

### Regular cleanup

Without a retention the DLQ grows until you delete entries. Give it one and it
cleans itself every time an entry is added:

```typescript
const queueManager = new QueueManager({
  redis: { host: 'localhost', port: 6379 },
  dlqRetention: {
    maxAge: 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000, // drop entries older than 30 days
    maxLen: 10_000, // keep at most the newest 10,000
  },
})
```

| Option   | Type     | Default | Effect                                              |
| -------- | -------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `maxAge` | `number` | none    | Entries added more than `maxAge` ms ago are removed |
| `maxLen` | `number` | none    | Only the newest `maxLen` entries are kept           |

Both are optional and can be combined; with neither set entries are kept until
deleted, retried or cleared. A standalone `DeadLetterQueue` takes the same
`DeadLetterQueueOptions` as its fourth constructor argument. A failed cleanup is
logged and never fails the `add()` that triggered it.

To purge on your own schedule instead, `purgeOlderThan(ms)` removes every entry
older than `ms` and returns how many it removed:

```typescript
const removed = await queueManager.getDLQ()?.purgeOlderThan(7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)
```

<Callout type='info' title='Failure isolation'>
  DLQ operations never block the main job flow — if adding an entry to the DLQ
  fails (e.g. a Redis hiccup), the error is logged and processing continues.
</Callout>

## FAQ

**Can I customize when jobs go to the DLQ?**
Indirectly — the trigger is `attemptsMade >= attempts`, so control it via the
`attempts` job option. To avoid the DLQ entirely: `enableDLQ: false`, raise
`attempts`, or handle errors inside `process()`.

**Different DLQs per job type?**
No — one DLQ per `QueueManager`. Use `filterByJobName()` to manage specific types.

**Export DLQ data?**
Yes: `const entries = await dlq.list(0, -1)` then serialize whatever fields you need.

- [Validation](/docs/queue/validation)
